Before we start

What your business needs in place.

AI projects fail on data and on definitions, almost never on models.

A definition of 'good enough'

Written down, before anything is built: what a right answer looks like, what a wrong one costs, and how often wrong is tolerable. Without it there is no way to tell whether the thing works, and every review becomes an argument about taste.

The data, and permission to use it

The documents, tickets or records it reasons over — and confirmation that using them this way is allowed. In banking, health and government this is the constraint that decides the architecture, so it comes first.

A provider account in your name

Anthropic, OpenAI or a cloud region. Billing sits with you, keys stay yours, and nothing about the system depends on my account existing.

Someone who can judge the output

A person who knows a good answer from a plausible one in your domain. They spend a few hours building the evaluation set, and that is the highest-leverage time anyone spends on the project.

A real volume estimate

Requests per day and how long an answer may take. Cost and architecture both hinge on it, and the gap between a hundred and a hundred thousand requests is a different system entirely.

No retainer to start a conversation, and no invoice for work that never got delivered.

Send it in one go and the clock starts.

  • What the product should do, in plain language

How it runs

Six steps, and you see each one.

  1. 01

    Frame

    What is the actual task, and is a model the right tool for it? Sometimes the answer is a database query.

  2. 02

    Prototype

    The smallest thing that proves it works, on your real data, inside days.

  3. 03

    Evaluate

    An evaluation set with your expert. From here, quality is a number rather than an opinion.

  4. 04

    Build

    The product around it: interface, retrieval, guardrails, fallbacks, monitoring.

  5. 05

    Cost and harden

    Per-request cost, rate limits, caching, and what happens when the provider has an outage.

  6. 06

    Ship and hand over

    Live, monitored, documented, with the evaluation suite so your team can keep measuring. The 30 days start here.

Right fit, wrong fit

Saves a call that would end in no.

A good fit

  • You have a real task, not a mandate to use AI
  • There is data, and permission to use it
  • Someone in-house can judge whether an answer is good
  • You want the cost modelled before committing
  • You would rather be told it is a bad idea than sold a build

Not a fit

  • The goal is to say the company uses AI
  • The data does not exist or cannot be used
  • Nobody can define what a correct answer is
  • You need a guarantee it is never wrong — nobody can give that

After launch

After it ships.

Model providers deprecate versions, change prices and ship better models on their own schedule. An AI product left alone for a year is running on something more expensive and worse than what is available. The Care plan is who tracks that.

Questions

The ones people actually ask.

Will you tell us not to build it?

Yes, and it happens regularly. That is what the discovery sprint is for, and it is priced so that outcome still leaves you better off than a build that quietly underdelivers.

Whose API keys and whose bill?

Yours, always. The provider account is in your name, the keys stay with you, and nothing depends on my account existing. I have no reason to want your inference bill running through me.

How do we know it is good enough?

An evaluation set built with your domain expert, run on every change. Quality becomes a number that moves up or down, which is the only way to have a sane conversation about a probabilistic system.

What if the model gets it wrong?

It will, sometimes. So the design question is what happens then: a fallback, a human in the loop, a refusal, or a clearly-marked uncertain answer. Which one is right depends on what a wrong answer costs you, which is why that number is a prerequisite.

Which model do you use?

Whichever fits the task, the cost and the residency rules — usually Claude, sometimes not, and it is a decision the discovery makes with numbers rather than a preference I bring with me.
